specPoints.text: understand how to use electrical conductivity and the acid-base character of oxides to classify elements as metals or non-metals
identify an element as a metal or a non-metal according to its position in the Periodic Table

primer.text: You already know from Atomic Structure how electrons fill the shells of an atom, and you can write arrangements such as 2,8,1. That picture is exactly what we need here, because the number of outer-shell electrons drives how an element conducts and how its oxide behaves. This note turns those two clues into a practical test for telling metals from non-metals.

lessons.title: Properties of metals and non-metals
lessons.opening: Sorting elements into metals and non-metals does not need a laboratory full of equipment: two quick tests settle most cases. Pass a current through the element and see whether it conducts, then check how its oxide treats acid and alkali. Good conductivity and a basic oxide point to a metal, while poor conductivity and an acidic oxide point to a non-metal.
keyPoints: Electrical conductivity and the acid-base character of oxides are the working tests for this sorting.
Metals hold one to three electrons in their outer shell, non-metals four to seven.
Metallic bonding comes from metal atoms losing outer electrons; non-metals bond covalently by sharing them.
Metals conduct well; non-metals are poor conductors, which makes the current test decisive.
Metal oxides are basic; the oxides of non-metals are acidic, with a few neutral ones.

low.restatement: An element that conducts well and forms a basic oxide is a metal; one that conducts badly and forms an acidic oxide is a non-metal.
low.analogy: It works like sorting mail by two stamps on the envelope: check the conductivity stamp, then the oxide stamp, and the pile is decided.
low.examPointer: Exam questions often hand you both clues and ask for the class; answer with the word metal or non-metal and one supporting property.

medium.restatement: Conductivity probes the electrons available to move charge, while how the oxide treats acid probes how the element bonds; the two tests agree because both trace back to the outer-shell electron count.
medium.analogy: Think of a border checkpoint with two officers: one watches the charge carriers moving through the element, the other watches how its oxide treats acid; both must reach the same verdict.
medium.examPointer: If a question says an element's oxide neutralises acid and the element lights a bulb, state that it is a metal and quote both observations as your supporting evidence.

check.stem: An unknown element conducts electricity well and its oxide neutralises dilute acid. How should it be classified?

options.text: Metal, because both tests point that way
options.explanation: Good conductivity and a basic oxide are the two metal markers together.

options.text: Non-metal, because some non-metals conduct too
options.explanation: Graphite is the famous conducting exception, but the basic oxide here confirms the metal verdict.

options.text: Metalloid, since anything that conducts sits on the border line
options.explanation: Border position, not conductivity, is what names a semi-metal.

options.text: Cannot be classified without its melting point
options.explanation: The two spec tests are sufficient; melting point is supporting evidence only.

check.stem: An element is dull and brittle, and its oxide dissolves in water to give an acidic solution. Which class fits?

options.text: Non-metal
options.explanation: Dull, brittle traits and an acidic oxide are the standard non-metal markers.

options.text: Metal, because all solid elements are metals
options.explanation: Several non-metals are solid, including sulfur and iodine; state alone never classifies.

options.text: Metalloid, because acidity always signals a border element
options.explanation: Acidic oxides are the ordinary non-metal signature; only table position names a metalloid.
options.misconception: oxide acidity misread as metalloid marker

check.stem: Which comparison row between metals and non-metals is correct?

options.text: Outer-shell electrons: metals hold one to three, non-metals four to seven
options.explanation: This matches the electron-arrangement comparison drawn in the note.

options.text: Outer-shell electrons: metals hold four to seven, non-metals one to three
options.explanation: The counts are reversed; metals hold the smaller number of outer electrons.

options.text: Bonding: metals share electrons, non-metals lose them
options.explanation: It runs the other way: metal atoms lose electrons to bond, non-metals share.

options.text: Melting points: metals low, non-metals high
options.explanation: Metals generally melt at high temperatures and non-metals at low ones.

check.stem: A solid element is lustrous and can be bent into shape, but a classmate calls it a non-metal because it is solid. What is the soundest reply?

options.text: It is a metal: malleability and a lustrous look outweigh state, which varies among non-metals too
options.explanation: The physical character is diagnostic here, and several non-metals are solid anyway.

options.text: Agree with the classmate: every solid is a non-metal
options.explanation: Most solid elements are metals, so state alone points the wrong way.

options.text: Agree, because metals can never be bent into shape
options.explanation: Malleability is one of the classic metal properties listed in the note.

options.text: Call it a metalloid because the class is disputed
options.explanation: A classmate's error does not create border status; the tests still say metal.

check.stem: Why do conductivity and oxide character work together as a classification pair?

options.text: Both reflect the same underlying outer-shell electron count, so the two verdicts normally agree
options.explanation: One test probes charge flow and the other bonding behaviour, and both trace back to how many outer electrons the element holds.

options.text: They test unrelated properties, so using both wastes time
options.explanation: They are two windows on one cause, which is exactly why agreement is convincing.

options.text: Conductivity alone decides, and the oxide test merely checks practical skills
options.explanation: Each test can mislead on its own; graphite is the classic conductivity exception.

lessons.title: Metals and non-metals in the periodic table
sourceHeadings: Metals & Non-Metals in the Periodic Table
Metals and non-metals in the periodic table
lessons.opening: Highlighted on the periodic table, the two families land in strikingly different territory: the vast majority of elements are metals, and they occupy the left of the table, with non-metals pushed to the right. A zig-zag line marks the boundary, and the few elements sitting on it behave like both camps at once, so they carry their own name.
keyPoints: On the periodic table, metals sit on the left and non-metals on the right.
The vast majority of elements are metals, which is easy to miss until the classes are coloured in.
A zig-zag line separates the metals from the non-metals across the table.
Elements bordering that line show traits of both sides and are called semi-metals or metalloids.
Position on the table is itself the classifier: identify the side, and you have named the class.

low.restatement: Left of the zig-zag line you are naming metals; right of it, non-metals; on the line, expect a semi-metal.
low.analogy: It is like a two-town border map: each side has its own mayor, and the villages straddling the line borrow from both councils.
low.examPointer: Exam sketches often shade the two regions; name a shaded element's class from its position before reading any of its properties.

medium.restatement: The table's layout mirrors the electron-arrangement story: metals on the left tend to lose their few outer electrons, while non-metals on the right gain or share to complete a shell.
medium.analogy: Picture a seating plan where the left rows share one snack habit and the right rows another; the aisle seats pick up both habits.
medium.examPointer: When asked to classify from position alone, quote the side of the zig-zag line first, then add one supporting property if the marks allow.

check.stem: An element sits immediately to the left of the zig-zag line on the periodic table. Classify it.

options.text: Metal, because the metals occupy the left of the table
options.explanation: Position to the left of the dividing line is the metal side of the table.

options.text: Non-metal, because everything near the line is a non-metal
options.explanation: Non-metals sit on the right; the immediate neighbourhood on the left is metallic.

options.text: Semi-metal, because every element near the line is one
options.explanation: Only elements that touch the line take the semi-metal label.

check.stem: Which statement about how the two classes share the periodic table is true?

options.text: Metals make up the vast majority of elements
options.explanation: Colouring the classes on a full table shows the metal region dominating the chart.

options.text: The two classes split the table roughly half and half
options.explanation: The metal region is far larger, so the split is nowhere near even.

options.text: Non-metals occupy most of the middle rows
options.explanation: The middle of the table is metallic; non-metals crowd the right-hand edge.

check.stem: What does the zig-zag line on the periodic table mark?

options.text: The division between the metal region on the left and the non-metal region on the right
options.explanation: That dividing role is exactly why the line is drawn.

options.text: The boundary between periods and groups
options.explanation: Periods and groups are table scaffolding, not the class divide.

options.text: The edge of the transition-metals block only
options.explanation: The line runs the height of the table separating both classes, not one block.

check.stem: An element borders the zig-zag line and shows a mix of metallic and non-metallic traits. Which term applies, and why is it used?

options.text: Semi-metal or metalloid, because such elements resist clean classification
options.explanation: The special term exists precisely for elements with characteristics of both sides.

options.text: Transition metal, because border elements belong to the central block
options.explanation: Transition metals sit inside the metal region and show no such mixed character.

options.text: Noble gas, because border elements are unreactive
options.explanation: Noble gases form the far-right group; nothing about the border implies low reactivity.

options.text: Alloy, because border elements mix both behaviours
options.explanation: An alloy is a mixture of metals, not a class assigned to a single element.
options.misconception: class term confused with mixture term

check.stem: With no property data at all, how do you classify an element shown only as a symbol on the table?

options.text: Read its position against the zig-zag line: left names it a metal, right a non-metal
options.explanation: Position is the designed classifier for this spec point.

options.text: Learn each element's class individually from a full list
options.explanation: The table's own geography does the work, so no list is needed.

options.text: Assume every element with a one-letter symbol is a metal
options.explanation: Symbol length says nothing about class; hydrogen sits on the left yet is a non-metal.

glossary.definition: Able to be bent and shaped without breaking; a typical property of solid metals.
Shiny and reflective in appearance; a characteristic physical mark of most metals.
Breaks or flakes rather than bending; a typical property of solid non-metals.
An oxide that reacts with acids; the oxide type typical of metals.
An oxide that reacts with alkalis; typical of non-metals, though a few non-metal oxides are neutral.
An element bordering the zig-zag line with traits of both metals and non-metals; also called a semi-metal.
